questions.stem: In the balanced equation C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O, how many moles of oxygen are needed to burn 2 moles of propane completely?
questions.explanation: The equation shows that 1 mole of propane requires 5 moles of oxygen molecules. Doubling the propane doubles every other quantity, so 2 moles of propane require 2 x 5 = 10 moles of oxygen.

distractorRationale.a: The propane amount was copied instead of applying the ratio
distractorRationale.b: This is the amount needed for just 1 mole of propane
distractorRationale.d: The number of oxygen atoms rather than oxygen molecules was counted

questions.stem: What mass of magnesium oxide is formed when 4.8 g of magnesium burns completely in oxygen according to 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO? [Mg = 24, O = 16]
questions.explanation: Moles of Mg = 4.8 / 24 = 0.2 mol. The ratio Mg : MgO is 2 : 2, that is 1 : 1, so 0.2 mol of MgO forms. The molar mass of MgO is 24 + 16 = 40 g/mol, so the mass is 0.2 x 40 = 8.0 g. The 3.2 g gain over the original 4.8 g is the oxygen that combined.

distractorRationale.a: 0.1 mol was used instead of 0.2 mol
distractorRationale.c: The mass of magnesium was doubled, incorrectly reading the coefficient 2 as a mass multiplier
distractorRationale.d: The ratio was taken as 1 : 2, doubling the moles of MgO

questions.stem: Calculate the mass in grams of carbon dioxide produced when 10 g of calcium carbonate reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid. CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2 [Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16]
questions.explanation: The molar mass of CaCO3 is 100 g/mol, so 10 g is 10 / 100 = 0.1 mol. The mole ratio of CaCO3 to CO2 is 1 : 1, so 0.1 mol of CO2 forms. With M(CO2) = 44 g/mol the mass is 0.1 x 44 = 4.4 g.

questions.stem: 0.5 mol of magnesium is burned in 0.3 mol of oxygen according to 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Which reactant is limiting and how many moles of magnesium oxide form?

options.text: Oxygen is limiting; 0.6 mol of MgO forms
Magnesium is limiting; 0.5 mol of MgO forms
Magnesium is limiting; 0.25 mol of MgO forms
Neither is limiting; 0.8 mol of MgO forms

questions.explanation: Reacting all 0.5 mol of Mg needs 0.5 / 2 = 0.25 mol of O2, and 0.3 mol is available, so oxygen is in excess and magnesium runs out first. Basing the calculation on the limiting magnesium and the 2 : 2 ratio, 0.5 mol of MgO is formed, leaving 0.05 mol of oxygen unreacted.

distractorRationale.a: This treats oxygen as limiting, but there is more oxygen than the 0.25 mol required
distractorRationale.c: The ratio was applied backwards, halving the magnesium instead of using the 1 : 1 relationship between Mg and MgO
distractorRationale.d: The moles of the two reactants were simply added, which has no chemical meaning

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 8.0 g but only 6.4 g of product is actually collected. The percentage yield is
questions.explanation: Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100 = (6.4 / 8.0) x 100 = 80 percent. Losses on filtering, transferring and drying, together with any side reaction, account for the missing 20 percent.

distractorRationale.a: The actual yield was multiplied by 10 rather than divided by the theoretical yield
distractorRationale.b: The difference of 1.6 g was mishandled, giving a rough guess rather than a calculated ratio
distractorRationale.d: The fraction was inverted, giving 8.0 divided by 6.4; a yield above 100 percent is impossible

questions.stem: What volume of carbon dioxide, measured at s.t.p., is produced when 25 g of calcium carbonate is completely decomposed? [Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16; molar volume at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm3/mol]
questions.explanation: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 has a 1 : 1 ratio. Moles of CaCO3 = 25 / 100 = 0.25 mol, so 0.25 mol of CO2 forms. Volume = 0.25 x 22.4 = 5.60 dm3. A quarter of a mole should occupy a quarter of the molar volume, which it does.

distractorRationale.c: 0.5 mol was used, as if the molar mass of CaCO3 were 50
distractorRationale.d: The molar volume was quoted without applying the 0.25 factor
